text:
What happened on the 11th: the primary Postgres instance ran out of connections at 09:12 and stayed that way for 41 minutes. The pooler had been sized for 200 connections since last summer, and the new export job opened 60 of its own on a schedule nobody had reviewed.

Requests that needed a write queued behind the pool and timed out at the gateway. Read traffic was fine the whole time, which is why the synthetic checks stayed green and nobody was paged until a customer wrote in.

What we are changing: the export job now takes its connections from a separate pool capped at 20, and it runs at 02:00 rather than during business hours. That change is already merged.

We are also adding a synthetic check that performs a write, because a read-only probe told us nothing useful for 41 minutes. That one is still open, and I would rather have it before the next export window.
note: Two genuine sections of two paragraphs each, both named by the author's own words, so headings are correct here.

text:
Why we are staying on SQLite: both it and LiteDB handle the volume we have, and both are a single file, so the choice came down to what we already know and what we can debug at three in the morning.

SQLite has a shell, a documented file format and twenty years of answers on the internet. LiteDB has a nicer C# API and we would write less mapping code, which is worth something but not worth learning a new failure mode this quarter.

What it means in practice: the repository layer stays as it is, and the migration runner keeps using plain SQL files under src/Scribe.Core/Storage/Migrations. Nobody has to change how they write a query.

We will revisit if the store grows past a few hundred megabytes, or if we need concurrent writers from a second process. Neither looks likely before the end of the year, and we would rather spend the time on the overlay.
note: A decision record with two author-named sections of two paragraphs, one spelled-out quantity and a path that wants code.

text:
How the hotkey pipeline works today: the low level keyboard hook lives in the tray process and posts to a channel, the recorder starts on the first key down and stops on key up, and the cleanup call runs on the thread pool once the buffer closes. Nothing in that path touches the UI thread, which is why the overlay can be busy without dropping audio.

The hook is a single global registration. Windows delivers it on the message loop of whichever process installed it, so a slow handler stalls every key on the machine, and that is the reason we do nothing in it beyond a write to the channel.

What I want to change: the recorder should start on hotkey press rather than on the first audio frame, because a cold microphone costs us about 200 ms and people notice it on short phrases.

I would also move the cleanup call behind a queue so a slow provider cannot stack requests when somebody dictates three times in a row. Neither change touches the hook itself, and both are contained in Scribe.Core.

text:
How the loop runs now: a recruiter screen, then a 45 minute technical call, then a half day onsite with three interviewers. The onsite is the expensive part for us and the tiring part for them, and we have been running it this way for about two years.

Feedback goes into the tracker within 24 hours of each stage, and the hiring manager writes their notes before the debrief rather than during it, which is the one habit that keeps debriefs to 30 minutes.

Where it breaks down: candidates hear nothing between the screen and the onsite, sometimes for two weeks, and we lose people in that gap to companies that move faster.

The other problem is that the onsite panel changes between candidates, so we end up comparing notes that were not taken against the same questions. I would rather fix the gap first, because that one loses us candidates we already wanted.

text:
Hotkeys. The default is ctrl plus alt plus space, held down while you speak. You can change it in Settings, and the app checks whether another program already owns the combination before it saves.

If the combination is taken, the tray icon shows a warning and dictation falls back to the menu item until you pick a different one. Nothing is silently swallowed.

Profiles. A profile applies when a particular app has focus and overrides the writing style, the model and the dictionary. Profiles are matched on the executable name, so a browser is one profile whatever site is open.

There is no inheritance between profiles. Anything a profile leaves blank comes from the global settings, which keeps the matching rules easy to reason about.

Storage. Transcripts and audio live under %LOCALAPPDATA%/Scribe. Audio is deleted 30 days after the transcript is written, and transcripts stay until you delete them.

Export writes a copy wherever you choose, and that copy sits outside the app's retention rules, so a folder you sync to OneDrive is your own responsibility.

text:
How the sanitizer decides. Every action declares a length band and the answer is measured against the input before anything else happens. A tone rewrite may land between 0.40 and 2.00 of the input length, a shortening between 0.10 and 1.10, and a structural conversion has just the runaway ceiling at 12.0.

Short selections are exempt from the ratio test for structural conversions, because converting 15 characters of prose to JSON legitimately multiplies the length. The absolute ceiling still applies, so a 5,000 character answer to a short selection is rejected anyway.

What happens on rejection. The original selection is returned unchanged and the palette shows the reason, so a caller that ignores the result cannot corrupt the document. A JSON conversion that fails to parse is rejected outright, because Replace is the primary button and an unnoticed failure is one keypress from landing in the file.

Dashes are the one check that compares output against input rather than against a fixed rule. The output may not carry more dashes than the input, which keeps the house style without rewriting a dash the author typed themselves.
